Module 11 — Final Precision Intraday Rulebook

The complete rulebook, checklists, and the testing and review protocol.

The claim of this module

This module does not introduce new concepts. Every rule below is a restatement of something already taught, in Modules 1–10, compressed into a form that can be read in under a minute before a trade and reviewed in a few minutes after one. If a rule here contradicts your memory of an earlier module, the earlier module's fuller explanation is correct — this is a summary, not a replacement.

By the end of this module you will be able to

  1. Recite the six core, non-negotiable principles that every other rule in this course derives from.
  2. Locate the specific rule governing any decision point in the trade sequence, organised by category.
  3. Run a pre-trade checklist that either clears a setup or correctly stands you aside.
  4. Run a post-trade review that distinguishes a correctly-priced loss from an execution mistake.
  5. Describe the backtesting → forward testing → demo → live pipeline and why no stage may be skipped.
  6. Journal a trade so that recurring mistakes become visible instead of invisible.

11.1Core principles

Every rule in §11.2 is a specific application of one of the six statements below. When a rule seems ambiguous in a live situation, resolve the ambiguity by asking which of these six it is protecting — not by guessing.

#PrincipleWhere it was established
1Direction is set on the 4H, refined on the 1H, executed on the 15M — never the reverse.Module 1, §1.4; Module 4, §4.2–§4.3
2A completed 15M candle close is the only form of confirmation this system accepts.Module 1, §1.6; Module 4, §4.6
3Stops and targets are structural, read from price — never arbitrary distances or manufactured to fit a number.Module 6, §6.2–§6.3
4No trade clears the sequence below a 1:2 reward-to-risk ratio, without exception.Module 1, §1.9; Module 6, §6.4
5Position size is solved backward from a fixed risk percentage and the stop distance — never chosen first.Module 9, §9.1
6Standing aside is a valid, frequent, and often correct outcome of running the sequence.Module 8, entire module

11.2The complete rule map

Sixteen rule categories, grouped into five functional clusters. Each table below states the rule and cites the module section it was derived from — nothing here is new; it is compressed.

Direction & context

CategoryRule
4H rules4H direction must show an unambiguous HH/HL or LH/LL sequence with no conflicting recent swing. This is Gate 1 — a binary pass/fail, not a preference (Module 2, §2.2; Module 4, §4.3).
1H rules1H must supply a location that satisfies ≥2 of origin, liquidity, or flip (Module 3, §3.2–§3.4; Module 4, §4.4). The 1H never overrides the 4H direction.
15M rules15M supplies confirmation only, never direction. No timeframe below 15M is used for entry refinement (Module 1, §1.7; Module 4, §4.6–§4.7).

Structure & liquidity

CategoryRule
S&R rulesZones are built from bodies, wicks, repeated reaction, displacement origin, or pre-expansion consolidation — never a single thin line (Module 3, §3.1–§3.2). Zone width is derived from the price behaviour that created it.
Liquidity rulesLiquidity is mapped as resting orders around obvious swing points before a trade is considered; a genuine sweep-and-reclaim strengthens a setup, an unresolved sweep against it weakens one (Module 3, §3.5).

Execution

CategoryRule
Entry rulesEntry occurs only after a completed 15M structure shift closes through the relevant level — never on an open or forming candle, never on anticipation (Module 4, §4.6–§4.8; Module 6, §6.7 on not chasing).
Stop rulesThe stop sits beyond the specific price level that disproves the trade thesis — never a fixed pip/point count chosen to fit a preferred position size (Module 6, §6.2).
Take-profit rulesThe target is the nearest genuine opposing structure — never widened or manufactured to clear the R:R minimum (Module 6, §6.3).
R:R rulesMinimum 1:2, calculated from actual entry/stop/target prices, before entry. Below 1:2 → stand aside, do not adjust the target to compensate (Module 6, §6.4; Module 8, §8.6).
Management rulesA continuous five-question loop (invalidation? momentum? breakeven/partial level? fading momentum? reversal signal?) replaces any clock-based exit. A reversal signal outranks unrealized profit (Module 7, §7.2–§7.5).

Protection

CategoryRule
No-trade rulesAny one of the sixteen stand-aside conditions (Module 8, Fig 8.1) is independently sufficient to end the sequence — conditions do not need to occur together.
Risk rulesPosition size = (Account × Risk %) ÷ (Stop distance × value per unit). Risk % is fixed in advance and derived from the specific prop firm's own limits, never a generic number (Module 9, §9.1, §9.7).
News/event rulesScheduled high-impact news is a stand-aside or flatten-exposure condition, not a sizing problem — a stop-loss does not guarantee fill price during a gap (Module 9, §9.5).
Correlation rulesPositions sharing an underlying driver are sized as one combined risk against a per-driver limit, never stacked independently (Module 9, §9.4).

Discipline

CategoryRule
Psychology rulesFOMO, revenge trading, overtrading, and confirmation bias are named and countered by one rule: the written sequence is the only permission to enter or exit (Module 8, §8.8).
Trade-review rulesEvery trade, win or loss, is logged and reviewed against the checklist that preceded it — see §11.4 and §11.6 below.
Check your understanding
A trader identifies a 4H uptrend, a qualifying 1H demand zone, and a valid 15M bullish structure shift. The calculated R:R to the nearest genuine opposing structure is 1:1.6. There is no scheduled news, no correlated exposure, and no other stand-aside condition present. According to the rule map, what should happen?

“Close to the minimum” is not the minimum. The R:R rule (§6.4, restated in §11.2) sets 1:2 as a hard floor, not a target to approximate. Reducing size does not fix an R:R shortfall — it only reduces the dollar amount of a trade that still fails the rule.

Correct. Principle 4 and §6.4 are explicit: no trade clears the sequence below 1:2, without exception. This mirrors Module 8's point that any single stand-aside condition is independently sufficient to end the sequence — the other gates passing does not offset the one that failed.

This is exactly the manufactured target §6.3 forbids. The target must be the nearest genuine opposing structure — selecting a different, more distant level purely to make the arithmetic clear the minimum is manufacturing the number, not finding it in the chart.

Check whether every one of the four gates in §6 and §8 independently passed, not whether the overall picture 'feels' good.

11.3Pre-trade checklist

Run every item before every entry, in order. This checklist does not award partial credit — a single “no” means stand aside, regardless of how strong the other items are.

How to use this checklist in practice

Write the answer down, even briefly — “yes” thought silently under time pressure is far easier to talk yourself past than “yes” written on paper or typed into a journal.

The final item (“I am taking this size because the checklist passed”) exists specifically to catch chasing and revenge trading (Module 8, §8.8) — answer it honestly even when every technical item has passed.

11.4Post-trade review checklist

Complete this for every closed trade — wins included — before taking the next one. This is the single habit most responsible for turning a strategy with a real edge into an account that survives long enough to realise it.

11.5Strategy failure vs execution failure

Every loss falls into exactly one of these two categories, and confusing them causes two opposite mistakes: abandoning a genuinely sound method after a normal losing streak, or persisting with a genuinely broken process because “the market was just against me.”

Execution failureStrategy failure (strategy-consistent loss)
What happenedA rule was skipped or bent — chased entry, moved stop, oversized, skipped a checklist itemEvery rule was followed exactly, and the trade still lost
What it meansThe written sequence would likely have produced a different outcomeThis is expected, priced-in behaviour — Module 1's expectancy math assumes real losses
Correct responseRetrain the specific discipline that slipped — identify it precisely using the post-trade checklistNothing changes after one loss; look for patterns over many trades, not single outcomes
Check your understanding
A trader takes a fully qualified long trade: every pre-trade checklist item passes, entry, stop, and target are exactly where the structure indicates, and the position is managed according to the five-question loop throughout. The trade is stopped out for a full 1R loss when a genuine, valid 15M bearish structure shift invalidates the setup. How should this loss be classified and treated?

Exiting earlier without a rule-based trigger would itself be an execution failure. The scenario states the five-question loop was followed throughout — there was no premature or overdue action. A stop that executes exactly where it was structurally placed, on a genuine invalidation, is the system working as designed.

A single loss, correctly taken, is not evidence the method needs revising. Module 1's honest expectancy arithmetic (§1.9) assumes a meaningful fraction of qualified trades will lose. §11.5 explicitly warns against treating one strategy-consistent loss as grounds to abandon or rebuild the method — that judgement requires a pattern across many trades.

Correct. The diagnostic question in Fig 11.6 (“was the checklist genuinely satisfied and management followed exactly as written?”) answers yes here. This is the expected, priced-in downside of a positive-expectancy system — recorded in the journal as data, not as a mistake to correct.

Ask the single diagnostic question from Figure 11.6 and follow where the 'yes' branch leads.

11.6Backtesting, forward testing, demo, and live execution

The sequence taught in this course is not ready for real capital simply because it is understood intellectually. Four stages exist, in order, each catching a different category of problem before it costs money.

StageWhat it testsWhat it cannot test
BacktestingWhether the rules, applied with discipline to historical charts, produce qualifying setups often enough to matter, and whether the qualifying setups have a reasonable, honestly-assessed win/loss patternWhether the trader can follow the rules under the pressure of live, unfolding uncertainty — hindsight removes that pressure entirely
Forward testingWhether the sequence can be identified and would have been followed in real time, with no hindsight and no capital at riskEmotional response to real money moving — paper trading materially understates the psychological pressure of live P&L
Demo executionOrder execution mechanics, platform behaviour, slippage assumptions, and emotional response to live-feeling but not-real P&L swingsThe specific pressure of capital that, if lost, cannot be replaced by resetting a demo account
LiveEverything — but only after the first three stages have shown consistent rule-followingNothing — this is the real test, which is exactly why it should not be reached prematurely
What each stage is actually measuring

None of the four stages exist to prove the strategy is profitable. Module 1 already establishes that a sound, positive-expectancy method can still show a losing stretch over any small sample. What each stage measures is consistency of rule-following under progressively more realistic pressure — that is the variable actually being tested, and the only one within the trader's control.

11.7Journaling

A journal entry is written for every trade — real or simulated, win or loss — before the next trade is taken. Without it, none of the four pipeline stages in §11.6 can be evaluated honestly, because memory of past trades is reliably distorted by their outcomes.

FieldWhy it is recorded
Instrument and sessionEnables later analysis of whether performance varies by instrument or session (Module 9, §9.8)
4H/1H/15M evidence at entryAllows a later, honest check of whether the checklist was genuinely satisfied or retroactively justified
Entry, stop, target, calculated R:RThe exact numbers used to compute expectancy over time, and to check for target manufacturing after the fact
Position size and % riskedConfirms the sizing formula (Module 9, §9.1) was actually applied, not adjusted by feel
Management actions takenReveals whether the five-question loop (Module 7, §7.2) was followed or overridden by impatience or fear
Outcome and R multipleRaw data for the expectancy calculation and for spotting patterns across many trades
Post-trade review answersThe strategy-failure/execution-failure classification (§11.5) for every trade, not just losses

11.8Reviewing winners and losers, and finding recurring mistakes

A journal that only examines losing trades misses two things: recurring mistakes hidden inside wins, and the difference between skill and luck. Both winners and losers are reviewed against the same checklist.

A win that breaks the rules is not a good trade

If a trade entered without full confirmation, sized outside the pre-committed risk percentage, or held past a genuine reversal signal still happens to win, the outcome does not retroactively make the process correct. Reviewing wins with the same rigor as losses is how a trader avoids learning the wrong lesson from a lucky outcome — and how rule-breaking habits get caught before they compound into a large loss.

A single loss, or a single rule deviation, is noise — it happens to every trader occasionally and proves little on its own. A recurring mistake is the same specific rule violation appearing across three or more journal entries: chasing entries, moving stops away from structure, oversizing after a loss, or skipping the same checklist item repeatedly. Patterns, not isolated events, are what the review process exists to surface.

Check your understanding
A trader's journal shows three separate trades over two weeks where the entry price recorded is noticeably worse than the 15M confirmation candle's close — in each case, the trader entered a few pips late after price had already started moving toward the target. All three trades still won. What does this pattern indicate, and what should happen?

Winning outcomes do not validate a rule deviation. §11.8 is explicit that a win achieved by breaking or bending a rule (here, entering later than the confirmed level) does not retroactively make the process correct — it means the trader got away with chasing three times, not that chasing is safe. The same habit will eventually enter on a move that reverses before target.

Correct. §11.8 defines a recurring mistake as the same specific rule violation appearing across three or more journal entries. The outcome of those three trades is irrelevant to whether the pattern is worth addressing — what matters is that entries are drifting from the confirmed price, which will eventually erode the R:R calculated at the checklist stage or cause a missed entry entirely.

§11.8 sets the threshold at three or more occurrences, not ten. Waiting for a much larger sample before acting on a clearly repeating, specific rule violation delays a correction that could prevent several more entries at worse-than-planned prices in the meantime.

Separate the outcome of the trades (win or loss) from whether a specific rule was actually followed.

11.9Practical — build your own working rulebook

Practical 11.1

Assemble a one-page rulebook you can actually use

Using the tables in §11.1–§11.2 and the two checklists in §11.3–§11.4, build a single page (physical or digital) that you could realistically read in under a minute before every trade.
  1. Write out the six core principles from §11.1 in your own words, short enough to fit on one line each.
  2. Copy the thirteen-item pre-trade checklist from Figure 11.3 exactly — do not shorten it yet; use it as written for at least ten qualifying setups first.
  3. Copy the nine-item post-trade review checklist from Figure 11.4 exactly, for the same reason.
  4. State, in one sentence each, the specific prop firm rules (or personal account rules) that determine your risk percentage per §9.7 — do not copy a number from this course or from anywhere else without checking it against your own actual limits.
  5. After ten logged trades, review your journal specifically for any checklist item that was never the actual cause of a stand-aside decision — that item may be redundant for your instrument and session, or it may mean you have not yet encountered the condition it is guarding against. Do not delete an item just because it has not fired yet.
Practical 11.2

Run one full post-trade review

Take the most recent trade you can find — real, demo, or from Module 10's worked examples — and complete the entire nine-item checklist from Figure 11.4 in writing, including an explicit strategy-failure/execution-failure classification per §11.5.

If you use one of Module 10's worked trades, note that both reached target, so the review will land on “strategy-consistent win” for every item — the value of the exercise is practicing the specific questions, not producing a dramatic finding.

11.10Vocabulary introduced or reinforced in this module

Core principleOne of six foundational statements that every specific rule in this course is a direct application of; used to resolve ambiguity when a specific rule's wording seems unclear in a live situation.
Pre-trade checklistA fixed, ordered list of conditions run before every entry; any single unmet condition means standing aside, with no partial credit for the items that did pass.
Post-trade reviewA fixed, ordered set of questions completed after every closed trade, win or loss, used to classify the outcome and detect rule deviations.
Execution failureA loss or suboptimal outcome caused by a rule being skipped or bent, where following the written sequence would likely have produced a different result.
Strategy-consistent lossA loss that occurred despite every rule being followed exactly — the expected, priced-in downside of a positive-expectancy method, not a signal that the method is broken.
Forward testingApplying the trading sequence to live, unfolding price with no capital at risk, to test whether the rules can be followed in real time without the benefit of hindsight.
Recurring mistakeThe same specific rule violation appearing across three or more journal entries, as distinct from a single isolated deviation.

11.11Summary — and the end of this course

  1. Six core principles underlie every specific rule taught across all eleven modules: direction flows 4H → 1H → 15M; confirmation is a completed 15M close; stops and targets are structural; the 1:2 R:R minimum has no exceptions; position size is solved backward from risk; standing aside is a normal, correct, frequent outcome.
  2. The sixteen rule categories in §11.2 map every decision point in the sequence to a specific, checkable rule — none of them require an in-the-moment judgement call made under pressure.
  3. The pre-trade checklist (13 items) and post-trade review (9 items) are meant to be used exactly as written, every time, not summarised from memory.
  4. Every loss is classified as either a strategy-consistent loss (the process worked, this outcome was always possible) or an execution failure (a rule was skipped) — confusing the two leads either to abandoning a sound method or persisting with a broken one.
  5. Backtesting, forward testing, demo execution, and live trading form a mandatory sequence, each stage testing a different kind of readiness; none may be skipped to reach live trading faster.
  6. A journal that records every trade — win or loss, real or simulated — and is reviewed with equal rigor in both directions is what turns isolated outcomes into visible, correctable patterns.
  7. This concludes the eleven-module course. The framework taught throughout — 4H direction, 1H location, 15M confirmation, structural stops and targets, honest R:R, disciplined risk management, and the judgement to stand aside — does not eliminate uncertainty. It makes that uncertainty measurable, and makes the risk taken against it deliberate and defined.
